title: The I Do: three approaches that don't work, and one that does
author: Craig Barton
summary: Drawing on watching over 100 maths lessons a month, Craig Barton critiques three common ways of running the teacher modelling phase, the I Do, and sets out the approach he now uses. Co-construction wastes time and confuses students, including a lesson where nine minutes of prompting yielded one correct student answer; the pure lecture gives clarity but no evidence students are listening; and the hybrid ends up chaotic, with students unsure of their role. His preferred sequence is a prior-knowledge check done beforehand with intervention outside the I Do, a Silent Teacher model of the whole process, and then narration with frequent checks for listening using Cold Call, Call and Respond and an Explain, Frame, Reframe pattern. The argument is that this keeps the clarity of a lecture while securing the participation that co-construction was after.
points: Barton rejects three I Do styles for specific reasons: co-construction becomes a guessing game, lectures give no evidence of listening, and hybrids blur student roles.
Checking prior knowledge before the I Do, with all responses visible and intervention kept separate, means the modelling can focus on a single new idea.
A silent model of the full process first gives students a calm overview before the steps are dissected.
The Explain, Frame, Reframe pattern with Cold Call and Call and Respond serves three purposes: it sustains attention, supports later diagnosis, and gives students regular success.
Barton admits he spent about 12 years on co-construction out of fear of telling students how to do something, giving the critique first-hand credibility.
quotes: I was scared to tell my students how to do something, so I would ask them questions they had little chance of answering correctly because the questions were about the very novel process they were about to be taught. At its worst, it is essentially a game of Guess what is in my head.
Sure, students may be silent and looking at us. They may even be nodding and smiling. But are they listening?

My experience of the hybrid approach is that it tends to be a bit chaotic. Instead of being the best of both worlds, it ends up being the worst of both, with students unaware of their ever-changing role in the process.
If my students’ prior knowledge is not secure, I intervene with an explanation, model and further practice. There is no point carrying on if the foundations are not in place.

Most of the time, I start the I Do with a silent model of the process from start to finish. I find this helps generate a calm focus to the I Do, as well as allowing students to see the entire process and begin to make connections.

First, they sustain students’ attention - if you know you could be asked to repeat what someone has just said at any point, and be held to account if you cannot, then quite simply you pay more attention.

In summary, this approach is designed to take the best features from the different types of I Dos I see during my classroom visits. We have the clarity and concision of the lecture approach, together with the increased student participation and cognitive engagement that underpins the co-construction approach.
